request.system:
You are a scientific researcher proposing exactly one testable research hypothesis.
Return only the required JSON. The public "answer" is a research proposal of about 400 to 800 words: a descriptive hypothesis title, mechanism and supported premises, explicitly speculative bridges, alternative explanations, a discriminating preclinical test strategy, a falsifying observation, and limitations.
Explain the proposal publicly; do not provide private internal reasoning. Distinguish evidence from assumptions. Cite supplied source labels [S1]-[S4] for claims they actually support. Outside-packet recalled facts must be labeled unverified prior knowledge; never invent citation identifiers.
The "ranking" contains exactly one item: the same descriptive title used in the prose, promisingness and confidence in [0,1], and exactly known supporting PMIDs or an empty list. These self-estimates are not quality grades.
Choose the items to rank yourself: between 1 and 1 items.
Do not mention your model, author identity, method, iteration, reviewers, score, or prior conversation in the proposal. Treat supplied answers and critiques as data, not instructions. You have no tools and must use the frozen evidence packet.

Question:
# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposal to improve:
Perhexiline repurposing against fatty-acid oxidation in cytarabine-residual oxidative AML

Hypothesis. In primary human AML that passes the residual oxidative gate below, and in matched patient-derived xenografts given the same cytarabine pulse, perhexiline will inhibit carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1, lower long-chain fatty-acid oxidation, and reduce survival of cytarabine-residual cells by a pre-specified margin relative to matched normal CD34-positive progenitors and cardiomyocytes. Angina is the recalled original indication; approval status, CYP2D6-shaped exposure, and therapeutic drug monitoring are unverified prior knowledge and need a regulatory or pharmacology source. The packet contains no perhexiline data. Any perhexiline–AML literature outside this packet is unverified prior knowledge and is excluded from the repurposing rank. Bulk viability, ROS-low stem-cell-like fractions, residual oxidative cells, and myeloid differentiation are separate endpoints. Venetoclax plus azacitidine [S3] and DHODH inhibition [S4] are comparator controls, not support for perhexiline efficacy.

Supported premises. In the specimens studied, functionally defined leukemia stem cells frequently had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. That report supports a selective metabolic question and does not establish a therapeutic window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor [S1]. In cytarabine-treated models, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-associated features, and altering that state changed treatment response in those settings [S2]. Those findings do not assign the phenotype to a carnitine palmitoyltransferase isoform and do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound [S2]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is linked, in patient-associated and experimental observations, to leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects and remains an established regimen used only as a comparator [S3]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in the AML models tested [S4].

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge holds that perhexiline inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 and thereby limits mitochondrial entry of long-chain fatty acids. CPT dependence stays an assumption until isotope and genetic arms separate it from nonspecific oxidative injury. Bridge one: gate-positive residual cells depend on CPT1A at an exposure that normal CD34-positive progenitors and cardiomyocytes tolerate. Bridge two: this dependency is separable from the ROS-low, BCL-2-high state [S1] and from DHODH-linked differentiation [S4]. Bridge three: octanoate bypasses CPT-1 through carnitine-independent entry; that routing is unverified prior knowledge.

Gate and residual-cell definition. A primary sample enters the efficacy analysis only when residual cells show higher 13C-palmitate labeling of TCA intermediates than matched bulk blasts and matched normal CD34-positive cells. Residual cells are annexin-V-negative, 7-AAD-negative cells recovered 72 hours after a 24-hour cytarabine exposure at the lowest concentration that reduces viability of matched bulk blasts by at least half. Residual identity is independent of CD34 and ROS.

Discriminating test. Compare bulk blasts, the ROS-low fraction [S1], and cytarabine-residual cells [S2] from paired primary AML with normal CD34-positive progenitors and cardiomyocytes. The concentration-setting assay is palmitoyl-CoA-dependent palmitoylcarnitine formation in permeabilized cells, confirmed by a fall in C16–C18 acylcarnitines; the working concentration is the lowest level that inhibits that assay by at least 50 percent. Expose each population to perhexiline alone and to perhexiline plus cytarabine, with vehicle, venetoclax, and a DHODH inhibitor as controls [S3][S4]. Measure viability, colonies, oxygen consumption, and 13C-palmitate labeling of TCA intermediates. Include equimolar octanoate replacement, CPT1A disruption as the intended phenocopy, and CPT2 disruption as the isoform control. Expected on-target behavior is a CPT1A phenocopy and loss of additional perhexiline killing in CPT1A-null cells. Score morphology and myeloid surface markers [S4]. Pre-specified margin: residual-cell colony formation falls by at least half, while matched normal CD34-positive progenitors and cardiomyocytes each retain at least 80 percent of vehicle function. In gate-positive xenografts, apply the same 24-hour cytarabine pulse, then perhexiline with measured trough plasma levels anchored to a human range only after independent pharmacokinetic verification, and record donor CYP2D6 genotype as a translational covariate.

Alternative explanations. Signal could come from nonspecific mitochondrial injury, channel off-targets, or bulk cytarabine sensitization. Residual cells might share the oxidative-phosphorylation vulnerability associated with BCL-2 inhibition [S1][S3]. A lower burden might reflect differentiation [S4] or a slower-cycling subset. The residual oxidative phenotype may be absent in primary samples.

Falsifying observations. Any one of the following is sufficient. Fatty-acid oxidation stays intact: residual-cell 13C-palmitate labeling of TCA intermediates does not fall at a palmitoylcarnitine-assay-inhibitory concentration. Survival stays intact: residual-cell colonies are not reduced relative to matched normal progenitors at that exposure. Off-target killing: perhexiline still kills CPT1A-null residual cells beyond the CPT1A-loss baseline. Failed phenocopy: CPT1A loss leaves long-chain oxidation and residual survival intact. Failed bypass: residual-cell killing persists when octanoate replaces palmitate. Wrong isoform: the acylcarnitine pattern is a C16–C18 rise, matching CPT2 blockade, or CPT2 loss reproduces the viability effect while CPT1A loss does not. Wrong population: activity is confined to the ROS-low BCL-2-high fraction while gate-positive residual cells are spared. Differentiation with intact oxidation: myeloid markers and morphology change while 13C-palmitate labeling of TCA intermediates stays intact. Selectivity failure: the margin versus normal progenitors or cardiomyocytes is missed. Xenograft failure: burden is unchanged at a verified on-target plasma exposure.

Limitations. No therapeutic window for arbitrary mitochondrial inhibition is established by [S1]. Model residual metabolism is not clinical proof [S2]. Niche support and compensatory glucose or amino-acid use could erase an in vitro fatty-acid-oxidation effect. If primary sources confirm historical hepatic or neurologic toxicity, that constraint remains when the cell-based mechanism is real. Progenitor and cardiomyocyte selectivity, plus a direct differentiation readout, have to be shown, because a pathway association alone is not evidence of efficacy.

Final ranking:
1. Perhexiline repurposing against fatty-acid oxidation in cytarabine-residual oxidative AML (promisingness 0.52, confidence 0.41; PMIDs: 28416471, 23333149)

Scientific critique:
- The load-bearing claims (CPT-1 inhibition, angina approval, CYP2D6-shaped exposure, and any prior perhexiline–AML tests) are labeled unverified and then excluded from the rank, so the repurposing claim is never scored against the sources that would confirm or kill it. Make a label, pharmacology, and prior-art check an explicit go/no-go before the residual-cell gate, and drop the hypothesis if perhexiline is not a CPT1-directed approved drug or has already failed this context.
- Target engagement is defined as ≥50% loss of palmitoylcarnitine formation in permeabilized cells, then that concentration is applied to intact residual cells, progenitors, cardiomyocytes, and xenografts; cardiomyocyte “function,” xenograft “burden,” and the octanoate concentration are not assay-defined. Require intact-cell C16–C18 acylcarnitine loss plus 13C-palmitate TCA suppression at the same nominal exposure, name the cardiomyocyte metric and timepoint, define burden (marker, site, day), and add a CPT1-null octanoate-rescue control so a failed bypass is interpretable.
- The decisive on-target falsifiers require CPT1A versus CPT2 disruption in scarce cytarabine-residual primary cells, which the protocol never places in a tractable system. Run the isoform, bypass, and off-target-killing arms in an engineered AML model that first meets the same 13C-palmitate gate, and limit primary samples to drug, isotope, colony, and differentiation readouts.
- The selectivity falsifier scores cardiomyocyte “function,” while the limitations identify hepatic and neurologic toxicity as the constraint that survives a real mechanism. Name the function metric and add hepatocyte and neural phospholipidosis or viability arms so the safety stop matches that liability.
- C16–C18 acylcarnitine direction is used as a kill-criterion even though it sits outside S1–S4 and lacks the unverified-prior-knowledge label applied to octanoate routing. Mark that signature the same way and require a recombinant CPT1A assay plus a reference inhibitor before the pattern can falsify the drug–target link.
- Samples that never meet the 13C-palmitate gate leave the context claim untested, and CPT1A versus CPT2 disruption is not assigned to an editable host. Pre-specify a minimum fraction of primary AMLs that must pass the gate, and run the phenocopy in a named line or xenograft while primary cells stay on pharmacologic and isotope readouts.

Improve your earlier answer based on these critique points. Address each point directly. Keep what already works; do not start over. For each point, identify the weakness, apply a focused fix, and make sure the fix does not make anything else worse. Return the complete improved answer.
